passage: On the edge of the small town of Hazaribagh, Ujjwal and Ira were the only two from their college preparing for the state service exam. They lived at opposite ends of town, and the bus between them took an hour. So they made a deal at the bus stand one Sunday: every night at ten, each would send the other one message: hours studied and the topic. Ujjwal wrote the first one in the dim light of his room: "3 hrs, geography." Ira replied: "2.5, history. Tomorrow 3." Some nights the numbers were small. When Ujjwal's mother was ill, he sent "1 hr" three nights running. Ira replied only, "Still counts." Neither wanted to be the one who broke the chain. After two months, the chain was sixty-one nights long.

qa.q: How long was the chain after two months?
How might Ujjwal have felt sending '1 hr' while his mother was ill?
qa.a: He likely felt worried about his mother and a bit ashamed of the small number, and relieved when Ira replied "Still counts."

qa.q: What small step could help them if one of them falls sick?
qa.a: Agree that even ten minutes of revision keeps the chain, so a hard week doesn't break it.

qa.q: How does Ira see the nightly messages?
qa.a: Ira sees them as a steady support; replying kindly keeps both of them motivated.

grounding: Two students preparing for the same exam report their nightly hours to each other and are motivated to keep the streak alive.
